UX Research

At an agency, research rarely looks like it does in textbooks. There's no dedicated research team, the timeline was agreed before anyone asked what users need, and the budget is usually tight. But skipping research doesn't save time. It just moves the cost to the end of the project, when a client sees the build and says "this isn't how our customers work."
So I treat research as something that has to fit the project, not something to skip. Here's how I approach it.
start-with-the-question-not-the-method
Start with the question, not the method
The most common mistake I see is picking a method first. "Let's do a survey" before anyone has said what we're trying to learn.
Nielsen Norman Group has a useful framework for this. They map methods along three dimensions:
Attitudinal vs. behavioral
: what people say versus what people do.
Qualitative vs. quantitative
: qualitative methods are better for "why" and "how to fix" questions, quantitative for "how many" and "how much."
Context of use
: whether people use the product naturally, follow a script, see a limited version, or don't use it at all.

They also tie methods to project stages. Early, to find direction: interviews, field studies, diary studies, surveys, concept testing. During design, to improve it: card sorting, tree testing, usability testing. After launch, to measure it: benchmarking, analytics, A/B tests, surveys.
That's how I plan. I write down the two or three questions we need answered, figure out the stage we're in, and the method usually picks itself.
stakeholder-interviews-come-first
Stakeholder interviews come first

On almost every project, research starts with the client. Requirement gathering with stakeholders and our system analysts tells me the business goals, the constraints and who the users are supposed to be.

It also tells me the assumptions. A university team might be sure students care most about program listings. A bank might assume customers want more features in the app. Those assumptions are what I want to test with real users.
talking-to-users
Talking to users
When I can get access to users, interviews are my main tool. NN/g's guidance shaped how I run them:
Ask about specific past events.
"Tell me about the last time you booked a hotel room" beats "How do you usually book hotels?" The second gets you an idealized version.
Ask for extremes.
Particularly frustrating or particularly smooth experiences are vivid, so people remember details.
Don't lead.
People will form an opinion about almost anything when asked. Pushing for answers creates opinions they didn't really have.
Don't ask them to design.
Interviews are bad for specific UI decisions, like menu types or button colors, and for predicting whether people would use a feature that doesn't exist yet.
Listen to what users say about their lives. Watch what they do with the design. Don't confuse the two.

For mobile apps with more than one kind of user, like a logistics app with customers and drivers, I talk to both groups separately. Their goals and context are completely different, and one group's needs can't stand in for the other's.
surveys-carefully
Surveys, carefully
Surveys are tempting because they're cheap and give you numbers. They're also easy to get wrong. A few rules I follow:
Use them for "how many", not "why." Interviews explain. Surveys measure.
Keep them short. Every extra question lowers completion and quality.
Ask about behavior and facts where possible, not hypothetical preferences.
Pilot with two or three people before sending it out. Confusing questions show up immediately.
testing-the-design
Testing the design

Usability testing is where research turns directly into design changes. NN/g's well-known guidance is that five users in a qualitative test find most of the usability problems you'd find with many more, and that the return drops quickly after that.

The important part of that advice is often skipped: it assumes you test, fix and test again. Several small rounds beat one big one. And if you have distinct user groups, each one needs its own participants. For quantitative studies with statistics, you need far more people, at least 20 according to NN/g.
On agency timelines, my version is simple: a few people, a clickable Figma prototype, three to five realistic tasks, and a quick round of fixes before the next review.
making-sense-of-it
Making sense of it
Raw notes don't change a design. Synthesis does. My go-to is affinity diagramming, usually in FigJam:
Everyone writes notes alone first.
One observation or quote per sticky. Working alone first reduces groupthink.
Cluster by content.
Group related notes, then label each group with a clear theme.
Don't throw away small clusters.
Outliers can be the most interesting finding.
Decide what to do.
For each theme: design change, open question, more research, or no action. Each gets an owner.
NN/g makes the point that the conversation while clustering matters more than the final diagram. That matches my experience, especially with developers in the room.
from-findings-to-screens
From findings to screens
This is the step that gets lost most often. A research deck full of insights that nobody acts on is wasted effort. So I connect each finding to something concrete:
A
user journey document
that shows where problems happen.
Design principles
for the project, written from the findings.
Specific screen changes
, with the finding noted in the Figma file next to the design.
When a client pushes back on a decision, being able to point to what users actually did is far more convincing than my opinion.
where-ai-helps
Where AI helps

I've built Claude Skills for UX research and user journey documents. They help me draft interview guides, spot leading questions, summarize transcripts and turn clustered notes into a first draft of findings. That saves real time on agency schedules. I still review everything against the source notes, because a summary that sounds right but misquotes a user is worse than no summary.
Running research after the design is already approved.
Treating stakeholder opinions as user research.
Recruiting only friendly or internal users.
Reporting findings without recommendations.
Testing once and calling it validated.

Sketching Will Help You A Lot

I spend most of my day in Figma, and I still start almost every project with a pen. Not because it looks nice in a process photo, but because it's the fastest way I know to find out which ideas are bad before I've invested in them.
This is the habit I push hardest when mentoring junior designers, and the one they resist the most at first.
the-problem-with-starting-in-figma
The problem with starting in Figma

Figma is a commitment machine. The moment you draw a rectangle, you're picking a width, a radius, a color, a font. Those choices feel small, but they pull your attention toward polish instead of the question that actually matters at the start: is this the right idea?
Bill Buxton's book
em
Sketching User Experiences

makes this point well. He treats sketching and prototyping as points on a continuum. Sketches come during early exploration and are meant to suggest and question. Prototypes come later and are meant to refine and commit. The trouble is when you skip straight to the second.

Buxton also argues that a sketch's ambiguity is where its power comes from. A rough sketch leaves room for interpretation, which invites other ideas. A polished screen looks finished, so people react to the details instead of the concept.
A sketch asks "what if?" A high-fidelity mockup says "here it is." Early on, you want the question.
what-the-research-says-about-making-many
What the research says about making many
One study I come back to often is by Steven Dow and colleagues at Stanford, titled
Parallel Prototyping Leads to Better Design Results, More Divergence, and Increased Self-Efficacy
. Participants designed web banner ads. One group made several prototypes in parallel before getting feedback. The other group made one at a time, getting critique after each.
The parallel group's ads performed better on click-through and were rated higher by experts. Their designs were also judged as more diverse, and the participants reported a bigger gain in confidence.
The lesson I take from it: exploring several directions side by side beats perfecting one and iterating on it. And sketching is by far the cheapest way to make several directions.
how-i-sketch
How I sketch
My setup is simple: A4 paper or a sketchbook, a fine black pen and a thicker marker. No pencil, because erasing turns it into polishing again.
My usual process:
Write the question at the top.
"How does a driver confirm a delivery?" or "What does a student see after logging in?" One question per sheet keeps it focused.
Crazy eights for breadth.
Fold the paper into eight panels and sketch eight different ideas in eight minutes. Most will be bad. That's the point.
Pick two or three.
Circle the ideas worth exploring, and note what's good about each.
Sketch the flow, not just the screen.
Buxton notes that sketching interaction is harder than sketching a static object because it has to show time. So I draw a few screens in sequence with arrows, like a storyboard.
Short notes on what's happening and what's still a question.
Only after that do I open Figma, and usually it's for lo-fi wireframes, not UI.
where-it-saves-the-most-time
Where it saves the most time
On agency projects, sketching earns its keep in a few specific places:
Kickoff and discovery.
Sketching during a workshop with the client and our system analysts helps everyone agree on what's being built before anyone argues about colors.
Complex flows.

Mobile apps with multiple user roles, like a trucking app with separate user and driver sides, or an exam review app with practice tests and progress tracking. The flow gets messy fast, and paper makes it visible.
Odd interactions.
An interactive mall map, a personality quiz for a drinks brand. Things with no standard pattern to copy.
Layout exploration.
Five homepage layouts on paper take minutes. Five in Figma take an afternoon.
sketches-are-social
Sketches are social

Buxton describes sketches as social things, meant to be shared and talked about. I agree. The best sketching sessions I've had are with developers and system analysts in the room, because they spot technical problems early and often suggest simpler solutions.
It also lowers the bar for everyone. A project manager who would never touch Figma will happily grab a pen and draw what they mean. That's often the moment a vague requirement becomes clear.
common-objections
Common objections
"I can't draw."
You don't need to. Boxes, lines, squiggles for text, a circle with an X for images. If someone can tell what the box is, it's good enough.
"It's faster in Figma."
For one screen, maybe. For eight different ideas, no. And the ideas you'd explore in Figma tend to be variations of the first one you drew.
"Clients won't take it seriously."
I rarely show raw sketches to clients unless we're sketching together in a workshop. They're a thinking tool for the team. What the client sees is the wireframe that came out of it.
"We have AI now."

I use AI tools a lot, including Claude Skills I've built for lo-fi wireframing. They're great at producing options fast. But choosing between options still needs a clear question and your own judgment, and sketching is how I get both.
tips-if-youre-starting-out
Tips if you're starting out
Set a timer. Short limits stop you from polishing.
Use a thick pen. You physically can't add too much detail.
Keep every sheet. Old sketches are a surprisingly useful record of why an idea was dropped.
Take a photo and drop it into the Figma or FigJam file so the thinking stays next to the design.
Sketch the empty, error and loading states too. They're usually forgotten until QA.

AI Is the Worst Thing That Happened to Creatives... Or Is It?

Every few weeks someone in a design group chat posts a screenshot of a generated landing page with the caption "it's over." And every few weeks I open Figma, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini and keep working, because the job isn't over. It moved.
So here's my take, up front:
AI is the worst thing that ever happened to one kind of creative work, and one of the best things to happen to the rest.

The kind it hurts is production done without judgment: resizing, filler copy, stock-looking visuals, the forty-variant banner set. The kind it helps is everything that needs taste, context and someone willing to put their name on a decision.
That isn't a vibe. Let's look at the receipts.
everyone-is-already-using-it
Everyone is already using it
The "should creatives use AI?" debate is mostly settled by behaviour, not argument.
Adobe's first Creators' Toolkit Report (Harris Poll, 16,000+ creators across eight countries, September 2025) found
of creators actively using creative generative AI, and
saying it helped grow their business or following.
The top uses weren't "make me a masterpiece." They were editing, upscaling and enhancement (

Figma's 2025 AI report, which surveyed 2,500 of its users, found

That matches how I actually work. AI is in my brainstorming, my first drafts of UX copy, my documentation, my research summaries, and the Claude Skills I build so the boring parts of a workflow run the same way every time. It's the most useful tool I've picked up in four years.
but-look-at-the-gap
But look at the gap
Here's the number that should get more attention than any adoption stat. In that same Figma report,
only 32%
of respondents said they can rely on AI's output. Designers were also noticeably less impressed than developers:
of designers reported being satisfied with AI tools versus
of developers, and only
of designers said it improves the quality of their work.
Fast is not the same as good, and the gap between them is exactly where a designer earns their pay.
That gap is the whole story. AI gets you to
something

very quickly. It doesn't know that the client's users are mostly on old Android phones, that the legal team will reject that headline, or that the "clean" layout it produced breaks the design system in three places. Somebody has to know that. That somebody is the job now.
Adobe's numbers say the same thing from the other side. Creators' top barriers were cost (
), unreliable output quality (
) and not knowing how the model was trained (

the-case-that-it-really-is-the-worst
The case that it really is the worst
I don't want to wave the fear away, because some of it is earned.
Jobs are shifting, and not evenly.
The World Economic Forum's
Future of Jobs Report 2025

, built from a survey of 1,000 employers covering 14 million+ workers, put graphic designers as the 11th fastest-declining job category, a role it had called "moderately growing" in its previous edition. If your work is mostly turning a brief into assets, that's a real threat, not a hot take.
Consent is a real grievance.
Adobe found
of creators worry their work will be used to train AI without permission. That isn't paranoia. It's a fair reaction to an industry that scraped first and asked later.
The legal ground is shaky for pure output.

The U.S. Copyright Office's January 2025 report on copyrightability concluded that prompts alone don't make you the author of what comes out. Protection needs a human who determined enough of the expressive elements. In March 2025 the D.C. Circuit agreed in
Thaler v. Perlmutter
that a work made autonomously by AI can't be registered, and the Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal in March 2026.
So if your plan is "prompt it, ship it, own it," the law is not on your side.
why-i-still-land-on-or-is-it
Why I still land on "or is it?"
Read those same receipts again and a different picture shows up.
That WEF report that made designers panic? The same coverage notes it ranked
UI and UX design as the eighth fastest-growing job category.
Demand didn't vanish. It moved toward people who design systems, flows and decisions instead of single artefacts.
The copyright rulings cut the same way. The Copyright Office explicitly said that
using AI to assist the creative process doesn't block copyright
, and that human selection, arrangement and modification can be protected. The D.C. Circuit said the human-authorship rule still rewards people who make work
with the help of
AI. The law isn't punishing creatives who use AI. It's punishing the absence of a creative.
And look at what creators actually use it for in Adobe's data: editing, enhancing, brainstorming. The people using these tools the most aren't asking to be replaced. They're asking for leverage.
what-actually-changed-in-my-day
What actually changed in my day
No made-up productivity percentages here, just the honest shape of it:
Blank pages are gone.
I rarely start from nothing. I start from three rough directions and spend my energy choosing and fixing.
Documentation stopped being the thing nobody does.
Handover notes, component specs and QA checklists get drafted by AI and corrected by me.
Judgment got more expensive.
When anyone can generate ten options, the scarce skill is knowing which one is right for
this
user and
brief, and explaining why to a client.
Junior work changed.
Mentoring now includes teaching people to distrust a confident output, not just how to use auto layout.
my-verdict
My verdict

AI is the worst thing that happened to creatives who were only ever paid for output. For everyone else it's a strong, flawed assistant that makes taste, context and accountability worth more, not less.
If you want a practical checklist, this is mine:
Use it for the first 60%, own the last 40%.
Generation is cheap. Editing, rejecting and refining is where you add value.
Keep a human hand you can point to.
Selection, arrangement, modification: that's where your craft and your copyright live.
Know your tool's training story.
If a client asks where a visual came from, "the AI made it" isn't an answer.
Never ship unread output.
Only 32% of builders say they can rely on it. Act like it.
Move up the stack.
Systems, research, flows and client conversations are where the growth is. Production alone is where the decline is.
Build your own workflows.
Prompts you reuse, skills you write, checklists you trust. The advantage isn't having AI. Everyone has it. It's having a process.
So, worst thing ever? Only if you let it make the decisions.

Three Fonts Are Greedy, Two Is Too Much, One Maybe

Every design review has that moment. Someone opens the type styles panel and there are four families in it: a display serif for headings, a geometric sans for the body, a "fun" script for the hero, and a monospace that showed up for one pricing table and never left.
Nobody planned it. It just accumulated. And that's my whole argument:
fonts are easy to add and expensive to keep.
Three is greedy. Two is usually more than the project needs. One, a good family used with discipline, is enough far more often than designers like to admit.
The title is a little dramatic on purpose. Here's the case with receipts.
even-the-typography-people-say-stop-at-two
Even the typography people say stop at two
This isn't just minimalist taste. Matthew Butterick, whose
Practical Typography
is one of the most practical references for working designers, puts it bluntly: "Most documents can tolerate a second font. Few can tolerate a third. Almost none can tolerate four or more."
Notice the framing. A second font is something a document
tolerates

. It's not a requirement. Butterick also says mixing fonts is optional, that pairing doesn't need the serif-plus-sans formula, and that "font mixing is most successful when each font has a consistent role in the document."
That last line is the test I use. If you can't say in one sentence what job the second font does that the first can't, it doesn't have a job.
A second font is something a design tolerates. A third is something it survives.
one-family-already-gives-you-a-whole-system
One family already gives you a whole system
The usual objection is "but I need contrast." Fair. But a single well-built family gives you a lot of contrast:
Weight:
light, regular, medium, semibold, bold, black
Size:
a real type scale, with big jumps for display and tight steps for UI
Width and optical size,
in families that support them
Case and tracking:
uppercase labels, tighter headlines, looser captions
Italic
for voice, emphasis and quotes
Colour and opacity
for hierarchy without changing the face
Variable fonts make this even easier. The 2024 Web Almanac found about
a third of sites (33–34%)
already use them. One file, a whole range of weights and widths, and every step stays in the same visual voice.

In my design systems work, the strongest hierarchy almost never comes from adding a typeface. It comes from a disciplined scale and clear weight rules. When hierarchy feels weak, the fix is usually spacing and size, not a new font.
every-font-is-a-performance-bill
Every font is a performance bill
Designers tend to treat fonts as free because they're free to pick in Figma. The browser doesn't agree.
The Web Almanac puts the
median web font file at about 39 KB
, with the 90th percentile at roughly
. That's per file. Every weight and style you add is another file unless you're using a variable font.
Web fonts are on about
of websites, so this is everyone's problem, not just enterprise sites.
web.dev's font guidance opens with the line I'd tattoo on every style guide: "The fastest font to deliver is a font that isn't requested in the first place."

Fonts also affect Core Web Vitals. Browsers "typically delay text rendering" until a web font loads, which can hit FCP and LCP. When the web font swaps in for a fallback with different metrics, you get layout shift, which counts against CLS.

Three families at three weights each is nine files fighting for bandwidth on a phone, before your hero image even starts loading. Preloading all of them isn't a fix either, since web.dev warns preload competes with other resources.
the-counter-argument-fairly
The counter-argument, fairly
"One font is boring. Brands need personality." Sometimes true, and I'll defend a second font in a few cases:
A distinctive display face for headlines
paired with a quiet workhorse for body and UI. This is the classic, and it works when the display font is used
only
for display.
Monospace for actual code or data,
where alignment and character distinction matter.
Multi-script products.
If you support languages your main family doesn't cover, adding a matching family isn't greed, it's accessibility.

Butterick even gives a shortcut for pairing: fonts from the same designer tend to work together. Superfamilies with matched sans and serif versions are a clean way to get two "fonts" that behave like one system.
What doesn't count as a reason: "the client liked it in a mood board," "it was trending on a font site," or "we needed something for the testimonial section."
And icon fonts? Font Awesome is still one of the most-used font families on the web, per the Web Almanac. I'd count it toward your budget, and these days I'd usually swap it for SVG icons.
Start with one. Earn the second. Treat the third as a design smell.
The checklist I'd hand any team:
Pick one family with range,
ideally a variable font with the weights and widths you need.
Build the hierarchy with scale, weight and spacing
before you consider another face.
Give any second font one written job,
for example "headlines over 32px only," and enforce it in the design system.
Count weights, not just families.
Two families at five weights each is ten files.
Ship WOFF2.
web.dev notes it compresses about 30% better than WOFF.
Subset
to the characters and languages you actually use.
Match your fallback metrics
(web.dev recommends
size-adjust
) so the swap doesn't shift the layout.
Audit quarterly.
Fonts creep in through one-off sections. Delete the ones with no job.
One font, used well, reads as confidence. Four fonts, used everywhere, reads as a team that never agreed on anything.

Is WebP the GOAT?

Every designer who has handed off a 4 MB hero PNG has been on the receiving end of the same dev message: "can you export this as WebP?" At some point WebP stopped being a format and became a personality. Convert everything, ship, feel fast.
So is it the GOAT? My take:
WebP is the GOAT of defaults, not the GOAT of formats.

It's the one you can pick without thinking and almost never regret. But AVIF often beats it on photos, JPEG XL is finally back in the conversation, and honestly the biggest wins on most pages have nothing to do with which file extension you chose.
the-case-for-the-crown
The case for the crown
WebP's résumé is genuinely strong.
Smaller than JPEG.
Google's own compression study found lossy WebP files are
25–34% smaller
than JPEGs at equivalent SSIM quality.
Smaller than PNG.
Google reports lossless WebP is
26% smaller
than PNG.
Transparency without the PNG tax.
Lossy WebP with an alpha channel is typically about
3× smaller
than the equivalent PNG, per Google's docs. For UI work, with product cutouts, shadows and soft-edged mockups, that's the killer feature.
It works basically everywhere.
caniuse puts WebP at about
global support. Desktop Safari got full support in version 16, and iOS Safari in 14.
The real-world data backs it up. The HTTP Archive's 2024 Web Almanac measured median compression across the web and found WebP images at
1.3 bits per pixel
, against
for JPEG and
for PNG. On the actual internet, not just in a lab, WebP is the most compact format in common use.
WebP is the format you reach for when you don't have time to think. That's a compliment, and it's also the ceiling.
the-challengers
The challengers
GOAT debates need rivals, and WebP has two good ones.
avif-the-stronger-player-with-a-slower-warm-up
AVIF: the stronger player with a slower warm-up
Jake Archibald's well-known AVIF comparison is still the clearest demo I've seen. His F1 car photo at acceptable quality came out at
74.4 kB as JPEG, 43 kB as WebP and 18.2 kB as AVIF.
On a gradient-heavy illustration, AVIF hit 12.1 kB where lossy WebP needed 26.8 kB.
Support isn't a blocker anymore either. caniuse lists AVIF at roughly
global support.
So why isn't AVIF automatically the champion? Archibald lists the trade-offs himself:
Encoding is slow.
At high effort settings it can take minutes per image in browser-based tools.
No progressive rendering.
AVIF arrives all at once. JPEG renders in passes and WebP renders top to bottom.
Lossless mode is weak.
In his flat illustration test, lossless AVIF was
against
for lossless WebP.
And here's the twist. That same Web Almanac data shows AVIF's real-world median at
1.4 bits per pixel
, slightly
higher
than WebP's 1.3, and up from about 1.0 two years earlier. Better codec on paper, not always better files in practice, because people encode it at whatever settings their pipeline defaults to.
jpeg-xl-the-comeback-story
JPEG XL: the comeback story
JPEG XL got pulled from Chrome in 2022 and was written off. Then, in October 2026, the Chrome team announced that
Chrome 155 decodes JPEG XL
, using a memory-safe Rust decoder (jxl-rs) and citing "30–50% better compression than JPEG," lossless support and built-in HDR. They pointed to years of developer demand as the reason.
It's not a default yet. caniuse currently puts JPEG XL at roughly
global support, with Safari still only partial. Watch it, but don't bet a launch on it.
the-uncomfortable-truth-format-is-rarely-your-bottleneck
The uncomfortable truth: format is rarely your bottleneck
Here's where I get a little contrarian. Google's own guide to optimizing Largest Contentful Paint says switching to a better format such as AVIF or WebP reduces resource load time, but notes that
load duration "tends not to be a significant bottleneck for most sites."
The delay often just moves somewhere else.
What hurts more in practice:
Lazy-loading the hero.
web.dev is blunt: "Never lazy-load your LCP image." Yet the 2024 Web Almanac found
of mobile LCP images still use native lazy-loading.
Images being the LCP at all.
of mobile pages have an image as their LCP element, which makes that one image the most important file on the page.
Shipping one giant size to every screen.
A perfectly compressed WebP at 3000 px wide is still a 3000 px image on a phone.
Priority confusion.
web.dev warns that giving high fetch priority to more than one or two images makes it useless.
A 400 kB JPEG at the right size, loaded early, can beat a 150 kB WebP that's lazy-loaded behind three scripts.
"Just use AVIF everywhere, it's 2026." Fair, and for photo-heavy sites like e-commerce, editorial or travel, a
picture
element with AVIF first and WebP as the fallback is the right call. The savings on hero photography are real, and the support is there.

But a lot of teams don't control their pipeline. A CMS, an image CDN or a plugin decides the encoder settings, and the Web Almanac numbers show what happens when nobody tunes them. If your stack can do AVIF well, use it. If it can only do one thing reliably, WebP is the one I'd pick.

WebP isn't the GOAT. It's the dependable veteran who shows up every game: great support, strong compression, good transparency, decent lossless. AVIF is the more talented player who needs the right coach. JPEG XL is the comeback kid we're watching from the bench.
My checklist for handoff and builds:
Default to WebP
for UI images, cutouts and anything with transparency.
Add AVIF first
for large photographic heroes when the pipeline supports it, with WebP as fallback.
Keep SVG for icons and logos.
No raster format beats a clean vector for flat shapes.
Size before you compress.
Export the sizes the layout actually uses and serve them responsively.
Never lazy-load the LCP image,
and give it priority. Only that one.
Check the output, not the extension.
Compare real file sizes and look at them zoomed in. A badly encoded AVIF is still a bad image.
Revisit JPEG XL
once Safari and Edge catch up.
The GOAT isn't a file format. It's the habit of asking "what does this image cost the page?" before you export it.

caseStudies/case-studies/seo-maxxing.md
SEO Maxxing

There's a whole genre of SEO advice that reads like a gym routine for your website. Hit 2,000 words. Put the keyword in the URL, the H1, the first paragraph and the alt text. Add five kinds of schema. Get a perfect Lighthouse score. Write an llms.txt. Repeat daily.
That's SEO maxxing: optimizing every visible muscle and hoping the algorithm notices. My take, as a designer who builds and ships small sites:
most of it is mewing for a robot.
On a small site, what actually moves results is boring and short: make pages worth finding, make them easy to crawl, make them not painful to use, then wait.
And I don't need to rely on my opinion here, because Google has written most of it down.
the-myths-google-already-debunked
The myths Google already debunked
Google's own SEO Starter Guide has a list of things that sound important and mostly aren't. Straight from the docs:
Meta keywords:
"Google Search doesn't use the keywords meta tag."
Keywords in your domain or URL:
they "have hardly any effect" beyond showing up in breadcrumbs.
Word count:
"The length of the content alone doesn't matter for ranking purposes."
Heading order:
for Search, "it doesn't matter if you're using them out of order." There's no ideal number of headings either.
Duplicate content penalty:
inefficient, but "not something that will cause a manual action."
E-E-A-T as a ranking factor:
Google's answer to that question is literally "No, it's not."
That last one surprises people. E-E-A-T (experience, expertise, authoritativeness, trust) is a framework for what good content looks like, not a dial you can turn up with an author bio widget.
If your SEO plan is mostly things Google has publicly said it ignores, you don't have an SEO plan. You have a ritual.
what-google-actually-asks-for
What Google actually asks for
The helpful content guidance is where the real signal is. It frames everything around
Who, How and Why
Who
made this? Is authorship obvious, with bylines that lead somewhere real?
How
was it made? Google even asks whether you explain how "automation or AI-generation was used to create content."
Why
does it exist? This is the one Google calls the most important. Is it there to help people, or "primarily made to attract visits from search engines"?

Their self-assessment questions are uncomfortably direct. Does the page provide "original information, reporting, research, or analysis"? Is it something you'd "want to bookmark, share with a friend, or recommend"? And my favourite: are you writing to a word count because you heard Google likes one?

For a portfolio or a small business site, this is great news. You have something big content farms don't: first-hand experience. A case study about a real project, written by the person who did it, is exactly what the guidance describes.
speed-matters-just-not-the-way-people-think
Speed matters, just not the way people think
Here's where designers and devs over-correct. Core Web Vitals are real. Google says plainly that "Core Web Vitals are used by our ranking systems." The targets, per web.dev, are:
LCP
(loading) at 2.5 seconds or less
INP
(responsiveness) at 200 milliseconds or less
CLS
(visual stability) at 0.1 or less
measured at the
75th percentile
of real visits, on mobile and desktop separately.

But read the next lines in the same doc. Good scores don't guarantee top rankings, and "Google Search always seeks to show the most relevant content, even if the page experience is sub-par." Page experience mostly helps when lots of pages are equally helpful for a query. Google also advises against chasing perfect scores just for SEO.
So yes, fix a 6-second hero image. No, don't burn a week shaving your Lighthouse score from 94 to 100 on a site nobody can find yet.
the-ai-era-temptation
The AI-era temptation
The newest flavour of maxxing is volume. Spin up fifty location pages, generate a blog post a day, let the model write the meta descriptions in bulk.
Google has a name for that:
scaled content abuse

, "when many pages are generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings." Their spam policy literally uses "using generative AI tools or other similar tools to generate many pages without adding value for users" as an example.
The tool isn't the problem. I use AI every day to draft, outline and edit. The problem is pages that exist only because they were cheap to make.

What about optimizing for AI Overviews and AI Mode? Google's own answer is that there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary." No special markup, no AI-specific text files. Just regular SEO fundamentals: crawlable, indexed, internally linked, content in actual text.
"Technical SEO matters. Schema, sitemaps and metadata are real." Absolutely, and I'm not saying skip them. Structured data can make a page
eligible

for rich results, and Google says it gives "explicit clues" about a page's meaning. A clear title and description affect whether people click. A broken robots.txt or a JavaScript-only page can make a site invisible.

But notice the wording: eligible, not guaranteed. Technical SEO is the floor that lets good content get found. It isn't a substitute for good content. Small sites tend to get the ratio backwards: twenty hours on plugins, two on the actual words.

SEO maxxing on a small site mostly means doing fewer, better things and waiting. Google itself says some changes take hours and others "could take several months," and suggests waiting a few weeks before judging a change.
My checklist:
Write pages only you could write.
Real projects, real process, real decisions. That's the "original analysis" Google asks for.
Make authorship obvious.
Name, role, an about page that's actually about you.
Nail the basics once.
Unique titles, honest descriptions, clean internal links, a sitemap, nothing important hidden behind JavaScript.
Fix the slow stuff that users feel.
Hero images, layout shift, laggy interactions. Aim for "good" at the 75th percentile, not 100.
Add structured data where it matches the page,
and treat rich results as a bonus.
Don't scale with AI for the sake of scale.
Use it to make a page better, not to make more pages.
Skip the rituals.
Meta keywords, keyword-stuffed URLs, word-count targets, "E-E-A-T scores."
Be patient.
Ship, measure in Search Console, wait weeks, then adjust.
The best SEO move I know is still the least exciting one: make something worth linking to and then don't get in its way.
